subject: technology
standards: Michigan Computer Science: Data and Analysis
essential_question: How can understanding data, media, and source responsibility help us explain, decide, create, or solve something that matters?
learning_objectives: Build a clear mental model of tables and charts through an explicit worked example, demonstration, text, or phenomenon.
Use subject-appropriate evidence or representation to communicate understanding of tables and charts.
Check, revise, or improve work about tables and charts using stated success criteria.
lesson_success_criteria: The learner completes the central task about tables and charts.
The learner gives evidence, reasoning, a model, or a documented process rather than an unsupported answer.
The learner checks or revises the work and can identify a next step.
materials: unit-specific source, model, manipulatives, safe materials, or approved digital tool
task_brief: This is day 2 of "Data, Media, and Source Responsibility". That is unit 5 in grade 5. Today is a worked-model trace about tables and charts. It takes about 40–60 minutes. It is one day's work, not the whole unit project. Your unit is working toward this: Create a transparent data story with cited or original media and an AI/source verification note. Today helps by working on tables and charts. Your unit also covers collecting simple data, tables and charts, image and media rights, and search strategies. Today is for practice. You are scored on finishing and being honest, not on getting it perfect.
primary_task: Use the whole example printed in activity_setup about tables and charts. Follow it one step at a time. Do not skip ahead. After each step, write what changed. Make a small table. Show what things looked like before and after each step. Now change one thing in the example. Guess what will happen. Then check. Was your guess right? Last, say the rule for tables and charts in your own words. Everything you need is printed in activity_setup. It has the exact case, what should happen, how to try it, checks, and a paper choice worth the same score. Do not wait for another handout or app. Keep today's work tied to your unit. Today is about tables and charts. It is part of "Data, Media, and Source Responsibility". Later days in this unit cover other things, like collecting simple data. Before you stop, do this check: In one concise response, show or explain the most important idea about tables and charts; then identify one check that would catch an error or weak claim. In grade 5, finish on your own. Write a reason for each main choice. If there were two ways to do it, say which one you picked and why.

execution_method.primary: Paper-first method: copy the short labels, annotate them, and complete the response in a notebook or any notes app. No download, installation, account, or internet access is needed.
execution_method.local_optional: A locally available word processor, spreadsheet, drawing tool, or slide editor may be used, but no particular brand or paid feature is required.
execution_method.check_path: Use the numbered specification and the package test/check criteria as a checklist; a parent or tutor can verify the cited labels without needing subject software.

test_cases.expected: one stated check with an observable pass condition
one limitation, unknown, or trade-off stated without inventing facts

debugging_target.observed_failure: An unsupported answer names the lesson topic but cites no labelled detail and has no observable way to check the proposed change.
debugging_target.target: Replace unsupported claims with evidence-linked claims, then add one pass/fail check for the proposed revision or decision.
debugging_target.passing_change: A reader can trace every conclusion to a printed label in the central input and can perform the stated check without outside materials.

equal_credit_alternative.method: A handwritten, typed, spoken-to-a-scribe, or labelled-diagram response earns identical credit when it addresses the same specification.
steps: Label three facts from the central input.
Explain how each fact connects to tables and charts.
State one revision or decision and its observable pass condition.
Name one limitation or missing fact without searching for outside information.
equal_credit_alternative.evidence_to_submit: Three labelled evidence links, the revision or decision, the pass condition, and the limitation or missing fact.

test_or_check_criteria: Your table has one row for each step and shows things before and after.
Each step has a short reason why it is right.
You changed one thing, guessed what would happen, and then checked.
You said the rule for tables and charts in your own words.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: Everything in this task runs in a sandbox or on paper. Never use a real password, passphrase, API key, account credential, access token, precise home location, or any real person's identifiable information — invent fictional values instead. Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. Any practice login used in an example must be obviously invented — a silly made-up name paired with a nonsense multi-word phrase — and must never be anything you or anyone in your family actually uses somewhere real. If a task seems to need something real, substitute a made-up stand-in and note the substitution.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any code, asset, or text you did not write must be openly licensed or supplied for this task, and must be cited in a comment or note naming where it came from and what you changed.
accessibility_options: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Allow typed, handwritten, spoken, drawn, manipulatives-based, or demonstrated responses when the standard permits.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
Preserve the learning target while adjusting quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode.
task_accessibility_provisions: You can do this with the keyboard only, no mouse needed. Text can be made bigger, and you may do it on paper instead of a screen.
Anything you have to study will also come as plain text, a described version, or a version you can touch.
You can take a break, stretch, or come back to this later. That does not lower your score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Never require a real password, private message, precise location, account credential, or identifiable image.
Use approved sites and tools; do not bypass filters, access controls, licensing, or terms of service.
Treat AI output as a draft to verify, not as an authority or a substitute for learner work.

media.suggestion: Optional diagram, map, worked example, source image, demonstration, or short clip supporting tables and charts.
media.fallback: Provide the same information as readable steps, alt text, transcript, tactile/concrete model, or teacher demonstration.

remediation: Reteaching for tables and charts follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for tables and charts, model it with a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the process for tables and charts works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of tables and charts, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking tables and charts mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply tables and charts under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work. Treat this as optional depth on tables and charts rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
